az_broken_rubber_boulder_main_lower_boul.blurb: A roadside boulder in the Sonoran Desert hills at Gates Pass, west of Tucson, and one of the first blocks you notice from the pavement. It holds eleven problems from V0 warm-ups to V7, with about half of them in the easy V0 to V2 band and a handful of hard, proud lines at the top end. The short walk-in makes it a quick stop rather than a day out. Winter is the comfortable season here, since the desert gets hot fast. Watch for jumping cholla and rattlesnakes around the landings, and keep to the established trails.

az_yakov_wall.blurb: A small northeast-facing sport wall in Euro Dog Valley, part of the Oak Flat side of Queen Creek Canyon in central Arizona. Eleven bolted lines, most only four or five bolts long, run from 5.9 up to 5.12, with 5.11 the most common range, so it suits climbers who already lead the low double digits. The rock is rough on the fingers. Most of the valley is known for bouldering, which makes this one of its few places to clip bolts.

az_praying_monk_the.blurb: A free-standing tower on the northern shoulder of Camelback Mountain in Phoenix, long treated as a rite of passage for local climbers and a common first multi-pitch outing. The rock is cemented mud and pebbles with plenty of knobby holds. Most lines are bolted or aid, with a few easy low-fifth and fourth-class options, several routes around 5.7, and a few harder ones at 5.10 and 5.12. The standard route is a single pitch, followed by a rappel back down. The base sits above the hiking trail, so you reach it after a scramble.
az_praying_monk_the.parking_note: Leave the car at the Echo Canyon trailhead lot off McDonald Drive; it is a busy lot and can take a few laps to find a space.
az_praying_monk_the.approach: Follow the standard Echo Canyon hiking trail up to the Headwall, then climb one of the Headwall routes (a short fourth-class scramble, with bolts) to reach the plateau where the tower stands.

az_gargoyle_wall_2.blurb: The sport face on the north side of Castle Rock, the fin above the Village of Oak Creek near Sedona. Eleven routes, all between 5.10 and 5.11, climb a gently overhanging panel covered in generous holds, giving pumpy, jug-hauling movement with a few crusty patches. Nearly all are bolted with lower-offs, which is unusual for this area where most lines are trad. It is a committed outing for the grade, since the walk takes around half an hour and ends in a scramble up a broken ridge.
az_gargoyle_wall_2.approach: Hike the usual path up to the col separating Castle Rock from North Castle Tower, then scramble the broken ridge until you reach the base of the panel.

az_the_middle_ages.blurb: A trad wall at the centre of the North Side of Volunteer Canyon, in the Sycamore Canyon country near Flagstaff. All eleven routes are traditionally protected, with one at 5.9, a few at 5.10, and most in the 5.11 to 5.12 range, topped by a single 5.13 line. It suits experienced leaders who like columnar basalt cracks and corners. The wall is reached from the rim, and finding the individual lines from above takes some route-finding. The canyon wall as a whole faces the sun, so spring and fall are better than summer.

az_west_side_down_the_hill.blurb: Roadside bouldering on the downhill side of Antelope Pass, along Highway 89 south of Page in northern Arizona. Eleven problems on large varnished blocks run from V0 up to V5, with the bulk in the V1 to V5 range and a couple of easy lines to start on. More widely spaced boulders lie farther down the slope, mostly to the north. It is a worthwhile stop if you are driving through rather than a destination crag.
az_west_side_down_the_hill.parking_note: Use the large dirt lot on the west, downhill side of Highway 89 and do not cross the road.
az_west_side_down_the_hill.approach: Walk north from the dirt lot to the big boulders; the walk is short.

az_beale_springs_west.blurb: A compact bolted wall on the edge of Kingman, in northwest Arizona. The face is nearly vertical, about 40 feet tall and north-facing, so it holds shade through the afternoon. Eleven sport routes span 5.7 to 5.11, with most in the 5.9 to 5.10 range, and the lines can be top-roped, which makes it handy for newer leaders and for short sessions. Anchors are fitted with hardware ready for lowering. The walk from the car is brief.
az_beale_springs_west.parking_note: Park in the lot behind the metal gate and chain at the old Camp Beale Springs site, north of downtown Kingman along Fort Beale Drive.
az_beale_springs_west.approach: From the lot, walk west under the overhead powerlines for about a quarter mile to the wall.
